The solutions of a homogeneous linear ODE form a [[Vector Space]], which is why the general
solution is written $c_1y_1 + c_2y_2$: that is a linear combination, and the $y_i$ have to be
[[Linear Dependence|linearly independent]] to count as a general solution. For a *system*
$\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$, the [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors]] of $A$ give solutions
$e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{v}$, and [[Diagonalization]] decouples the system into independent scalar
equations. See [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]].

---

An equation whose unknown is a **function**, related to its own derivatives. $y' = 2y$ does not ask
for a number, it asks which function is its own derivative doubled. Almost every physical law is
one of these, because laws state how a quantity *changes* and the quantity itself has to be
recovered by integrating.

Solving one means finding the function. Since the general solution of an $n$th order equation
carries $n$ arbitrary constants, it names a whole family of curves, and **initial conditions pick
one out**: one condition per constant.

## Classifying it, which is how you pick a method

| Question | Values | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Order** | highest derivative present | how many constants the answer has |
| **Linear?** | is $y$ and are its derivatives to the first power, with no $y y'$ or $\sin y$ | linear equations have a complete theory, nonlinear ones do not |
| **Homogeneous?** | is the right hand side zero | decides whether you need a particular solution |
| **Coefficients** | constant or functions of $x$ | constant coefficients reduce to algebra |
| **ODE or PDE?** | one independent variable or several | a [[Partial Differential Equations|PDE]] is a different course-block |

## The method table

| Equation | Method | Note |
|---|---|---|
| First order, separable | separation of variables | introduced in [[CALCULUS 2]] |
| First order, linear | integrating factor $e^{\int P\,dx}$ | introduced in [[CALCULUS 2]] |
| Linear, constant coefficients, $=0$ | characteristic equation | [[Homogeneous ODE]] |
| Linear, constant coefficients, $\neq 0$ | complementary plus particular | [[Non-Homogeneous ODE]], [[Undetermined Coefficients]] |
| $ax^2y'' + bxy' + cy = f$ | substitution $x = e^t$ | [[Cauchy-Euler]] |
| Coupled first-order system | eigenvalues of the matrix | [[Systems of Differential Equations]] |
| Variable coefficients, no closed form | power series | [[Series Solutions]] |
| Qualitative behaviour only | draw it | [[Phase Portrait]] |

[[CALCULUS 2]] meets the first two rows as an application of integration and hands the rest here.
The through-line for all of them: **an ODE is solved by integrating**, so every technique in
[[Integration Techniques]] is a prerequisite.

## Why linearity is the dividing line

A linear differential operator is a [[Linear Transformation]] on a space of functions. That single
observation buys the entire theory: solutions of the homogeneous equation form a subspace (so
linear combinations of them are solutions), the general solution of the inhomogeneous equation is
one particular solution plus that subspace (the same statement as $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$), and
in the system case a change of basis decouples everything. **Nonlinear equations have none of this**,
which is why the toolkit ends there and [[Phase Portrait|qualitative methods]] and numerical
methods take over.
